Uber Freight CEO Rebecca Tinucci took to LinkedIn to tout the company’s third quarter financial performance, which still is a long way from operating profitability.
As Tinucci said in her published remarks, “two things can be true at the same time.”
Her comments highlighted gross bookings of $1.768 billion, which is a record for the group. It also was a 34% improvement over the third quarter of 2026.
Sequentially, Uber Freight (NYSE: UBER) revenue also was up from the second quarter figure of $1.583 billion, an 11.6% gain.
But those higher revenues also came with another operating loss, $33 million.
That wasn’t what Tinucci focused on in her LinkedIn remarks. Instead, she cited other statistics that were not in the Uber parent company’s prepared statement regarding its earnings.
Tinucci said the approximately 35% year-over-year in revenue was “supported by an exceptional 36% volume increase in our U.S. & Canada brokerage.” She added that occurred even though the market featured “relatively flat freight volumes across the industry.”
Revenue per load was up about 8% year-over-year, Tinucci said. Loads per day per head, considered in the brokerage business to be one of the key measures of productivity, was up about 10% from the third quarter of 2025.
In its history, Uber Freight, whether it reported its bottom line as operating income or EBITDA (as it did until recently) has reported positive income only a handful of times.
The road to profitability at Uber Freight remains a tough one. $UBER pic.twitter.com/2cR2bu1yrr — John Kingston (@JohnHKingston) November 4, 2026
Tinucci said of the latest report that Uber Freight is “making steady progress toward profitability.” The adjusted operating loss of $33 million is an 18% improvement over a year ago.
But Tinucci added that it came only after the company had spent $17 million on “improved employee liquidity programs and targeted investments.”
Another number touted by Tinucci was segment operating margin as a percentage of gross bookings as being improved from a year ago.
The operating income loss, while narrower than a year ago, widened sequentially from $24 million in the second quarter. That meant that the operating income as a percentage of gross bookings deteriorated to negative 1.9% from negative 1.5% in the second quarter. However, it was stronger than the negative 3.1% from a year ago.
While Uber Freight is loosely described as a digital broker, a good chunk of its business is the legacy Transplace business, which it announced it was acquiring in 2021. That business features a TMS system for shippers.
Tinucci described the company’s “vision for Transportation Orchestration” as seeking to “help our customers continuously and autonomously improve their transportation networks. It’s a lofty vision – one that requires us to combine insights from the $18B freight we manage with our technology, logistics expertise and access to capacity. And one that will, no doubt, take us many quarters to achieve.”
Tinucci returned to the “two things can be true at one time” theme to wrap up her LinkedIn message.
“Uber Freight delivered our strongest quarter since I joined, posting great revenue, volume, and profitability gains,” she said. “At the same time, it is only more clear to me how much farther we have to go.”
Uber Freight did not garner a mention on the parent company’s earnings call with analysts. But CEO Dara Khosrowshahi did tweet a message of support to Uber Freight on X.

Boehringer Ingelheim is building up its China strategy, inking a deal to develop new cancer treatments with Sino Biopharmaceutical just weeks after opening an R&D facility in Shanghai.
Boehringer Ingelheim is doling out $358 million in upfront and near-term payments to potentially pick up six preclinical antibody-drug conjugates or T cell engagers from Sino Biopharmaceutical.
China’s Sino—which recently adopted the global name SBP Group—will also be eligible to earn up to $7 billion from potential option-exercise and milestone payments, plus tiered royalties, according to a Wednesday release . The partners initially linked up in 2024, making this their second oncology collaboration.
The newest deal will grant Boehringer the option to license six early-stage cancer programs stemming from several SBP Group subsidiaries: five biologic programs from antibody drugmaker LaNova Medicines in Shanghai and a sixth coming from Beijing Tide Pharmaceutical.
Under the terms of the deal, SBP Group will conduct early development for all programs. After certain undisclosed clinical milestones are met, Boehringer will be able to opt in on each asset. For four of the candidates, Boehringer could gain exclusive rights except in a few Asian countries, while the option for the remaining two programs would include global rights.
The collaboration is an example of Boehringer’s China strategy in action, the company said in the Wednesday release. Just last month, the German drugmaker opened a new R&D center in Shanghai that is designed to bolster early-stage clinical development efforts in the country. Boehringer has pledged to invest in Chinese innovation over the long term.
At the top of the year, Boehringer inked a deal worth up to $1.26 billion with Shanghai-based Simcere Pharmaceutical. That pact centers around SIM0709, an investigational bispecific antibody designed to target both TL1A and IL-23 in order to treat inflammatory bowel diseases.

First-Ever Supercharged Shelby Mustang GT350R Needs a New Owner, No Other Like It Exists
46 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Typically, when a car wears an “R” in its nameplate but only on certain, select versions, it means it’s in a huRRy. It’s Rapid. Its motor puts out more poweR and toRque, it acceleRates quickeR, and hits higher top speeds, therefore it’s fasteR. In other words, it’s like a Race car, but Road legal. Which is gReat – for those who have one. Pete Wojtowicz has one, and it only needs a drop or two or Red to be the greatest All-American pony car ever.
If you spend enough time talking cars with Mustang guys, the Shelby GT350R always comes up with a certain grin. Back in 1965, Carroll Shelby took a simple Ford fastback and turned it into a proper track bully. The regular K-code street version was already plenty quick , but that extra R meant pure business, giving weekend racers a stripped, loud, high-winding V8 machine built to embarrass much pricier European sports cars.
Across four generations, that basic recipe never really changed. You bought the standard Shelby when you wanted a factory warranty and a fun Sunday cruiser, and you stepped up to the R when you only cared about going fast. Because production numbers stayed tiny in every era, spotting one on the street is rare. Recently, though, a really wild sleeper popped up near Indianapolis, courtesy of Lou Costabile, the classic car YouTuber who documented it on camera.
It’s a 2011 Ford Mustang Shelby GT350R owned by Pete Wojtowicz (if the name doesn’t sound familiar, I’ll have you know he also owns a 1-in-12 Shelby Mustang GT350H in Red with gold stripes, and a 2024 Shelby Series II – the first one ever built).
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile At first glance, his 2011 GT350R looks like a clean throwback to 1965, finished in white with painted blue stripes, blue mirrors, a smooth nose, and blocked quarter windows carrying Carroll Shelby’s autograph. Under the scooped hood sits a 5.0-liter V8 with a Ford Racing Whipple supercharger.
Standard supercharged 2011 GT350 builds made 525 horsepower, while ordering the R race tune pushed output to 625 horsepower, and this particular car actually put down 650 horsepower on the dyno. It runs a McLeod dual-plate clutch, a short-throw 6-speed manual shifter, and a one-piece aluminum driveshaft. Shelby brakes, pillar gauges, sequential taillights, and a screaming center exit exhaust make it an absolute riot on pavement.
The backstory on this Mustang is where things get really good. It was the second to last example of the first 20 VIP cars reserved by Shelby American executive Gary Patterson strictly for employees and close friends. Folks call this batch the “Encore Series” because 2011 was the last Shelby GT350 model Carroll Shelby gave his blessing to. Its first owner was Warren Faris, a high-ranking official at Shelby American back then.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile When the bosses of Ford Racing and Special Vehicle Technologies heard Warren was getting the first R upgrade, they made custom GT350R door sills just for him. Every other 2011 GT350R was left unbadged, needing paperwork or a dyno run to prove what it was. That, and the fact that is puts down more horsepower than all that came in its wake, makes this spectacular GT350R a one-off.
After passing on $100,000 MSRPs in 2011, Pete found this gem in Fort Myers, Florida, 3 years ago. The bigger Shelby Mustang story started in 1965 when Ford boss Lee Iacocca asked Carroll Shelby to build a Corvette fighter, before adding the big block GT500 in 1967. First generation GT350 production ran from 1965 to 1970, opening with 562 cars in 1965, including 36 factory GT350R racers. Their 289 cubic-inch V8 packed 306 horsepower, or 350 horsepower in R spec, backed by a 4-speed manual.
Those early cars earned their reputation on the track right away. Ken Miles drove GT350R prototype 5R002 to victory in Texas in February 1965, kicking off three straight SCCA B Production championships from 1965 through 1967. When new, base prices ran at $5,950 for the 1965 Shelby Mustang GT350R. Prototype 5R002 fetched a record $3,850,000 at a Mecum auction in 2020 – the highest price of any Mustang ever sold publicly.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile After a 46-year break, Shelby American revived the name from 2011 to 2013, converting 159 Mustangs in 2011, 132 in 2012, and 36 in 2013. Buyers paired 6-speed manual or automatic transmissions with a 5.0-liter V8 (the first-generation Coyote legend) making 525 in standard GT350 guise or 625 horsepower and 575 lb-ft (780 Nm) in the 80 R-rated, steroid-fed examples.
It wasn’t a standalone model , but a post-title upgrade on an existing Mustang GT, with the upgrade costing a whopping $33,995. For reference, note that the standard donor vehicle started at $30,890. With other Shelby add-ons, a new car left the assembly line with an ear tag of $83,000 or more.
Ford took over from 2015 to 2020, building 3,647 track-focused GT350R model, with a 5.2-liter flat-plane crank V8 (the nefarious naturally aspirated “Voodoo” powerhouse) delivering 526 horsepower and 429 lb-ft (582 Nm) through a Tremec 6-speed manual. The GT350R-C won the 2016 IMSA championship.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile For 2025 and 2026, Shelby American returned on the S650 chassis, capping yearly builds at 562 GT350s and 36 GT350R track brawlers alongside a Trans Am racer. Its Whipple supercharged 5.0-liter V8 Coyote pairs with 6-speed manuals or 10-speed automatic gearboxes to make 830 horsepower in R trim.
This 15-year-fresh example isn’t afraid to put some wrinkles on the tarmac, as Pete joyously feathers the throttle just enough to make rear-wheel grip scream for mercy. He’s not overdoing it, though, nbut even the slightest touch of the l oud pedal pushes the occupants deep in the seats – watch the end of the video to see how the owner gave Lou a big smile with nothing but torque and supercharger whine. Oh, and by the way, if you like this car more than a lot, ask Lou for Pete’s details – it is for sale.

U.S. rail traffic increased 3.5% in the week ending Oct. 31 compared with the same week in 2025, the Association of American Railroads said Wednesday. Carload traffic rose 3.0%, while intermodal volume increased 3.9%.
Seven of the 10 carload commodity groups recorded year-over-year gains. Metallic ores and metals led with an 18.3% increase, followed by forest products at 9.3% and motor vehicles and parts at 9.1%. Chemicals rose 7.9%, farm products excluding grain and food increased 6.9%, petroleum and petroleum products gained 2.5%, and nonmetallic minerals edged up 1.1%.
Miscellaneous carloads posted the largest weekly decline, falling 12.2%. Grain traffic dropped 8.3%, while coal slipped 0.4%.
For the first 43 weeks of 2026, total U.S. rail traffic increased 3.8% from the same period last year. Intermodal volume rose 4.7%, outpacing a 2.7% gain in carloads. Grain remained the strongest year-to-date carload category, up 10.1%, despite its weekly decline. Metallic ores and metals increased 8.9%, and petroleum and petroleum products rose 7.9%. Coal was the only carload category below its year-earlier level, down 1.6%.
Across the nine reporting U.S., Canadian and Mexican railroads, combined weekly traffic increased 4.3% from the same week last year, according to the AAR. North American carloads rose 3.9%, while intermodal traffic gained 4.7%. Through the first 43 weeks of 2026, combined North American traffic was up 3.3%.
Why it matters: The weekly increase extended a positive year-to-date trend, with total traffic up 3.8% through the first 43 weeks of 2026.

Range Rover is pulling the plug on its two most affordable models, the Evoque and Velar, as a new entry-level EV steps in.
Range Rover drops Evoque and Velar for the new GT EV
For decades, the Range Rover name was viewed as a status symbol, mostly used by wealthy buyers, high-powered executives, and even royalty.
That started to change with the launch of the Evoque in 2011 and the Velar in 2017, making the iconic British luxury brand a little more accessible.
In the US, the 2026 Range Rover Evoque starts at $49,900, and the Velar starts at $61,600. That’s considerably less than the Sport and flagship Range Rover SUVs, which start at $83,700 and $107,400, respectively.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Range Rover’s accessible luxury era is reportedly drawing to a close. Martin Limbert, Range Rover’s managing director, confirmed to Autocar that the Evoque and Velar will officially be discontinued, with production set to end in 2027.
While it has no direct replacement planned, the new Range Rover GT will serve as the brand’s new entry-level vehicle.
Range Rover GT prototype (Source: Jaguar Land Rover)
Range Rover revealed the GT in July, presenting it as the fifth and newest member of the lineup. Unlike the distinct SUV design Range Rover has built the brand on, the GT is a low-slung grand tourer.
The electric GT is “a captivating new expression” of the brand, Range said, describing it as “the most technologically sophisticated” model it’s ever designed.
It’s expected to be among the first vehicles based on JLR’s new EMA platform. Initially, the Range Rover GT will launch as a battery-electric vehicle (BEV), but Range Rover plans to add a full-hybrid (HEV) option later in the lifecycle.
Production of the Range Rover GT is set to begin in the first half of 2027 at JLR’s Halewood, UK plant, following the flagship electric SUV and smaller Sport EV model (shown below).
The Range Rover GT is expected to start at around $90,000 with an EPA range of at least 300 miles when it goes on sale as a 2028 model. In the UK, it will likely be over £75,000 ($100,000).
Range Rover’s flagship electric SUV starts at $140,450 in the US, and the smaller Sport EV will likely be a bit cheaper at around $120,000 to $130,000.
At $90,000, the electric GT isn’t what most would consider an “entry-level” vehicle, but it’s part of Range Rover’s push into higher-end, more profitable models.

MDC's XT22HRT Travel Trailer Offers Aussie Toughness, Three Living Zones, and Massive Battery Power
31 photos
Photo: MDC USA
The RV market is overflowing with offers, so manufacturers that want to stand out definitely have to go all out on features and creature comforts to attract buyers. To stay ahead of the competition, new-to-market brands are not only trying to come up with innovative features but also go larger and essentially turn their models into true luxury homes on wheels.
That’s what MDC has done with the XT22HRT travel trailer, the latest addition to the company’s Off-Grid Extreme lineup and the largest model it has even built for the US market. Scheduled to arrive at dealerships across the country in early 2027, the new flagship is 22 feet (6.7 meters) long and is designed to offer rugged capabilities for off-road travel, an elegant and spacious three-zone interior, and impressive self-sufficiency credentials.
For those who are not familiar with the name, MDC is an Australian RV manufacturer that’s only new to the US market. In its home market, it has been building travel trailers, hybrid RVs, and off-road campers since 2005. Like most Australian-built RVs, MDC units are designed to tackle the most challenging landscapes and handle long journeys in off-grid locations.
Since 2021, MDC USA has brought that Australian off-road innovation to American overlanders and outdoor explorers with rugged travel trailers built for freedom, comfort, and exploration.
Photo: MDC USA MDC USA founder and President Vaughan Hindley has said that the new XT22HRT has been designed to respond to customer demand for a larger travel trailer. “The XT19HRT has become our most popular Off-Grid Extreme model, and there has been clear demand for us to take that concept further with more space, capability and comfort,” he said. “This style of layout has also proven incredibly popular across our Australian ranges. We know how well it works in the real world, and I genuinely think U.S. travelers are going to love what we have created with the XT22HRT.”
The XT22HRT is the eighth model in the manufacturer’s Off-Grid Extreme range and takes the idea of off-grid travel to the next level with more solar and battery capacity, more interior living space, and greater comfort thanks to several new amenities for extended stays away from civilization. Some of these include a cold weather pack, dual-zone Truma heating and cooling, internal and external kitchens, three distinct interior living zones, and nearly 2,000 pounds (907 kg) of cargo carrying capacity.
Offering an interior floorplan that measures 22 feet (6.7 meters) in length, the XT22HRT actually comes in at 29.6 feet (9 meters) in overall length from the drawbar to the rear bumper and is 7.7 feet (2.3 meters) wide and 10.3 feet (3.14 meters) high. It’s a dual-axle travel trailer built on a galvanized steel chassis, and what makes it a great option for overlanding enthusiasts is its sturdy yet lightweight construction that combines a welded aluminum frame with aluminum composite panels.

PARIS — French shipbuilder Naval Group has unveiled an 8,000-ton drone carrier concept designed to deploy fleets of surface, aerial and underwater drones .
“The return of high-intensity conflict and the emergence of hybrid naval warfare require a new vision. Naval Group answers with a new concept ship: SCX 26,” Naval Group wrote in a Tuesday post on X.
Still in its blueprint stage, the company unveiled its concept at the Euronaval defense show in Paris. Naval Group said in a press release that it developed the carrier based on new operational requirements, lessons learned from recent wars, and medium- to long-term technological advancements.
The idea is for the carrier to be what the French group calls an “operational hub of a hybrid fleet,” able to launch a variety of drones for missions ranging from intelligence gathering to anti-submarine warfare.
According to the theoretical capabilities outlined, the ship would measure 170 meters in length and weigh 8,000 tons, with a crew of 150. The carrier is expected to reach a maximum of 30 knots and roam the seas for more than 8,000 nautical miles. Naval Group plans for the ship’s core onboard weapon to be composed of “over 100 vertical launching system silos of various classes and an electromagnetic gun capable of rapid fire.”
Separately , the French shipbuilder on Tuesday also signed a contract with the French Armament General Directorate (DGA) to begin manufacturing an unmanned combat underwater vehicle (UCUV) demonstrator intended for the French Navy.
While the project was officially launched in 2023, Naval Group since 2016 has self-funded the development of this extra-large underwater drone. During a nine-month study in 2023, the company said it tested Controlled Decision-Making Autonomy, an “onboard brain” algorithm that coordinates mission parameters and enables unmanned systems to autonomously execute challenging operations while adhering to human-defined mission boundaries.
The UCUV demonstrator’s first sea testing is slotted for 2028 to “validate a mid-term operational response” to new areas of conflict, Naval Group said.

Bench-Seat Sleeper: 1967 Ford Fairlane Hides Dual-Quad Surprise Under the Hood
14 photos
Photo: Duffy's Classic Cars/eBay
Introduced as a full-size car in 1955 , the Fairlane was Ford's flagship model until the Galaxie arrived in 1959. In 1962, the Fairlane joined the emerging intermediate car market. Like most mid-size cars of the era, it also joined the muscle car wars.
As a bread-and-butter automobile, the Fairlane came standard with an inline-six engine, while the option list included an assortment of small-block V8 powerplants. In 1966, however, Ford added the 390-cubic-inch (6.4-liter) FE to the lineup. Additionally, the larger 427-cubic-inch (7.0-liter) V8 found its way under the Fairlane's hood for homologation purposes.
Rated at 425 horsepower, the R-code V8 was fitted into only 57 cars that year. While low, the number allowed Ford to homologate the powerplant (and the Top-Loader four-speed manual gearbox) for NHRA and IHRA Super Stock racing.
The following year, the Fairlane became available with the W-code 427, which featured a four-barrel carburetor and delivered 410 horsepower. However, the R-code engine remained on offer for customers who wanted to take the Fairlane racing. It's still unclear how many of these dual-quad factory race cars were built, but the consensus is that fewer than 100 left the assembly line.
These cars are obviously very desirable today, and one has recently surfaced in Cedar Rapids, Iowa. It's a fully restored example in Ivy Gold Green, and it's looking for its next caretaker.
I haven't seen many 1967 R-code cars on the auction block recently, so this hardtop is a pretty big deal. The fact that it looks like it just rolled off the assembly line is a big plus. Many of these cars were raced back in the day and then spent decades in long-term storage.
The metallic green paint looks gorgeous, while the chrome trim is flawless. If you're a fan of color-keyed interiors, this Fairlane delivers; the cabin has the same shade of green as the body, with dark green inserts on the seats. Speaking of which, this Fairlane 500 was equipped with a front bench seat. It also has the cheap steel wheels, so it's pretty much a sleeper.
But make no mistake though, this Fairlane is not your grandma's weekend rig. It still packs the 427 R-code and Top-Loader combo, which was quite expensive back in the day. Priced at $1,752.20, it added a 72% premium to the Fairlane's base sticker. The R-code went for over $4,000 at the time (that's more than $41,000 in 2026 dollars), which explains the low production number.
Speaking of which, the seller says this Fairlane is one of 72 units built with this drivetrain. Most sources, however, claim that Ford actually put together 92 examples. Typo or mistake aside, this R-code Fairlane is super rare, with fewer still in solid condition today.
The muscle car is being auctioned off by a dealership , and bidding has reached $50,300 with less than two days to go. The reserve is still in place, and I have a feeling that the seller is aiming for a six-figure sum.

Moderator Amber Mac makes a point with, from left, Schneider Electric’s Shitiz Agarwal, Vale’s Jeff Gaulin, Agnico Eagle’s Andre Leite and PwC’s Subo Chatterjee. Credit: Toronto Board of Trade
Posted By: Colin McClelland November 4, 2026
Ontario’s push to accelerate mine approvals risks running into a shortage of skilled workers that could inflate construction costs and stall investment, executives from Agnico Eagle Mines (TSX, NYSE: AEM) and Vale’s (NYSE: VALE) base metals unit warned Wednesday.
Agnico’s underground mining school at Macassa in the province’s north drew 500 applicants within two weeks for 25 training places, while Vale sees billions of dollars in potential Ontario projects competing for a limited workforce, executives told a Toronto Region Board of Trade conference.
“We’re gonna run out of miners before minerals,” Jeff Gaulin, Vale Base Metals’ vice-president of corporate affairs, said. “We are not graduating enough mine engineers to meet our ambitions.”
The warnings expose a practical limit to Ontario’s effort to turn faster permitting into a mining expansion. More predictable approvals can help attract capital, but companies still need trained crews, competitive electricity and enough construction capacity to deliver projects on time and earn investors a return.
The discussion came two days after Ontario added Mayfair Gold’s (TSXV: MFG; NYSE-A: MINE) Fenn-Gib gold project to its One Project, One Process framework, making it the fourth development selected for coordinated provincial reviews. The designation aims to accelerate approvals; it does not itself authorize construction.
Training bottleneck
The workforce challenge is partly a shortage of training capacity, rather than simply a lack of interest in mining careers, Agnico’s Ontario operations vice-president Andre Leite said.
That interest reflects a wider shift . A Mining Industry Human Resources Council (MiHR) survey of 3,000 Canadians aged 15 to 24 found 42% would consider a mining career, up eight percentage points from 2023. Positive impressions now exceed negative ones, although mining still trails technology and health care.
Agnico is training 25 people per quarter through its Macassa school in Kirkland Lake. But limits on how many apprentices can train alongside qualified tradespeople constrain its ability to expand the workforce, Leite said.
“We do have youth in Northern Ontario. They want the jobs,” he said. “But we didn’t train them in the past to be in these positions.”
Northern Ontario could need about 20,000 more workers as the industry grows and existing employees retire, he said, without specifying a deadline for that requirement. Training skilled tradespeople takes years, making it difficult to respond quickly once projects receive approval.
“When we look at the pool of talent that we have, it’s just not deep enough,” he said. “So we need more people. We need more training.”
Labour accounts for 40% to 50% of Agnico’s costs, Leite said. Access to people who can execute projects is therefore central to investors’ questions about whether developments will arrive on schedule and within budget.
Automation can help improve productivity, but Leite cautioned against expecting technology to advance quickly enough to close the entire workforce gap. Operating mines need to serve as training grounds for the next generation of workers, he said.
Gaulin described the scale of demand through a conversation with an unnamed Canadian provincial premier about expanding a mining engineering program. Asked how many graduates Vale would hire from a class of 40, the company’s answer was all of them for the next decade, with their school fees covered, he said.
Efforts to attract students include Franco-Nevada’s (TSX, NYSE: FNV) partnership with The Northern Miner Group on an education portal highlighting Canadian post-secondary programs and scholarships. CEO Paul Brink discussed the initiative on TNM’s podcast in March, stressing the need to attract more people to mining.
Power costs
Electricity is another test of whether Ontario’s ambitions translate into competitive operations, Gaulin said. He urged the province to renew its northern industrial electricity rebate for the long term and expand it.
The Northern Energy Advantage Program’s current five-year term ends March 31. It supports large industrial electricity users in the north, including mining operations.
Matthew Rae, Ontario’s associate minister of energy-intensive industries, acknowledged the approaching expiry in a subsequent discussion. He said he was working with Northern Economic Development and Growth Minister George Pirie on potential future versions of the program, but announced no renewal.
Rae also acknowledged the challenge of aligning transmission and generation with proposed northern mines. Ontario’s relatively clean electricity supply can attract investment, but the province would not match Quebec’s hydroelectricity prices, he said.
Keeping smelters supplied
Ontario Mining Association president Priya Tandon urged governments to give existing mines and expansions the attention being directed towards flagship projects.
Permitting delays can leave companies paying to retain scarce contractors while waiting for authorization to proceed. Releasing those contractors risks losing them to another project, she said.
Red Tape Reduction Minister Andrea Khanjin said Ontario is reviewing 375 economic permits, extending its reforms beyond projects selected for special treatment. The work includes allowing activities to proceed under prescribed rules and developing an online system for proponents to track applications, with mining permits first in line.
Tandon also warned that Sudbury’s energy-intensive smelters need competitive operating costs and a steady supply of feed from existing operations and nearby mineral developments. Protecting that processing capacity is essential to supplying both domestic industry and allied countries, she said.
“Well, what keeps me up at night is ensuring that they’re consistently fed,” she said.
Investment discipline
Gaulin put Vale’s potential Ontario projects over the next five years at about $5 billion (US$3.6 billion). That was an opportunity rather than an investment commitment: he warned that Vale and other companies moving ahead together could bid up costs and struggle to find enough people to build.
Both executives welcomed closer cooperation between governments and industry. Leite still ranked permitting as the largest obstacle to investment decisions, followed by costs and access to skilled workers.
But strategic importance alone will not persuade boards to approve construction, Gaulin said. Projects must deliver attractive net present values and internal rates of return.
“Mining CEOs don’t get rewarded by their boards and investors for building strategically important assets,” he said. “They get rewarded for the disciplined capital allocation of projects that give the best returns.”

Battery-electric cars took a record 37% of Germany’s new car market in October, according to data released today by the Kraftfahrt-Bundesamt (KBA), the country’s federal motor vehicle authority. That’s 94,086 BEVs, up 79.5% from 52,425 a year earlier.
For the second month in a row, German buyers registered more fully electric cars than gasoline and diesel cars combined. And with two months left in the year, Germany has already blown past the auto industry’s EV forecast for all of 2026.
A record month in a record year
The overall market barely grew in October. Total new car registrations rose 1.7% to 254,492 units, which means the EV growth came straight out of combustion cars.
Gasoline car registrations crashed 40.5% to 38,516 units, a 15.1% share. Diesel fell 21.6% to 23,882 units, or 9.4% of the market. Add them up and pure combustion cars made up just 24.5% of new registrations, 12.5 points less than BEVs alone.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Plug-in hybrids slipped 7.9% to 28,499 units (11.2%). So plug-ins accounted for about 48% of the German market last month, and the average CO2 emissions of new cars dropped 21.1% year-over-year to 79.4 g/km.
As we reported this summer, BEVs became the most popular powertrain in Germany for the first time in June with a 28.4% share. They’ve kept climbing every month since: 32.4% in August, 34.5% in September, and now 37% in October.
Battery-electric cars outsold gasoline and diesel combined in Germany in October. Data: KBA
Through the first ten months of the year, Germany has registered 698,230 BEVs, up 60.7% year-over-year. That’s about 28.2% of the 2,476,290 new cars registered in 2026 so far, up from roughly 19% for the full year 2025.
BEV share of new car registrations in Germany by month, 2026. Data: KBA
And the industry didn’t see it coming. In December, the VDA, Germany’s auto industry association, forecast about 693,000 BEV registrations for all of 2026. Germany passed that in October. At the current pace, it’s on track for somewhere around 875,000 by the end of the year.
The subsidy is working
The biggest driver is Germany’s new EV incentive, which applies retroactively to cars registered since January 1. It pays €3,000 for a new BEV, bought or leased, and up to €6,000 for lower-income households with children. Households with taxable income above €80,000 (€90,000 with kids) don’t qualify.
The program targets private buyers, and that’s exactly where the KBA data shows the jump. Private registrations rose 20.6% in October, while commercial registrations fell 8.2%. Private buyers now make up 40.7% of the market.
Germany has been here before. The government killed its previous EV incentive overnight in December 2023, and BEV sales fell off a cliff in 2024. This time, the money is going to the buyers who need it most, and it’s moving the needle fast.
BYD edges out Tesla, Chinese brands surge
Tesla’s German numbers swing wildly with its quarterly delivery cycle. In September, the end of the quarter, it registered 12,552 cars (+268.7%) and the Model Y was the best-selling car in Germany. In October, it registered only 2,932, which is still up 290.9% but from a tiny base, for a 1.2% market share.
Year-to-date, Tesla is up 206.1% to 47,742 registrations. That’s a big rebound from a terrible 2025, but BYD is now slightly ahead with 47,961 (+216.1%). BYD registered 5,173 cars in October (+54.3%), though the majority of its German sales are plug-in hybrids, not BEVs.
The other Chinese brands are growing even faster. Leapmotor registered 3,661 cars in October, up 288.6%, and is at 19,705 for the year. Xpeng was up 284.4% to 1,380 units, and SAIC’s MG was up 48.5% to 4,140.
Volkswagen Group still owns the top of the EV charts, though. Through September, the Skoda Elroq was Germany’s best-selling EV with 30,845 units, ahead of the Tesla Model Y (29,464) and the VW ID.3 (24,352).
German automakers aren’t cashing in
The EV boom is happening during one of the worst years in the history of Germany’s auto industry.
In October, the VW brand’s German registrations fell 4%, Audi dropped 8.4%, Porsche lost 5.7%, and Opel crashed 24.1%. BMW was flat (+0.1%), and Mercedes was the exception, up 8.5%. VW is still by far the biggest brand in Germany with an 18.2% share, but it’s down 5.6% for the year.
Year-over-year change in German registrations by brand, October 2026. Data: KBA
Last week, Volkswagen Group reported a €5.9 billion operating loss for the third quarter , its biggest quarterly loss since Dieselgate, driven by a writedown of its Porsche stake, weak sales in China, and thin EV margins. The group has already approved a plan to cut 100,000 jobs and close several German plants. Mercedes cut its 2026 car margin guidance to 2-3% last week, mainly because of China.
It’s not a product problem. VW’s new ID. Polo is sold out with over 30,000 orders , BMW has over 50,000 orders for the Neue Klasse iX3 , and the Elroq leads the German EV market.
Electrek’s Take
Germany is proving what we’ve been saying for years. Give buyers EVs they can actually afford, and they switch fast. Fully electric cars went from about 19% of the market last year to 37% in October, and the country beat the industry’s full-year forecast with two months to spare. That’s not a slow transition.

20 photos
Photo: Toyota
Toyota has found another way to sell off-road capability without forcing customers into an expensive trim. For model year 2027, the Sequoia full-size hybrid sport utility vehicle gains a Trailhunter-branded package for the SR5 grade. Said package adds $3,500 to the final price, making it a very different proposition from the overly expensive TRD Pro specification.
If you ask me, Toyota knows what it's doing here. The SR5 Trailhunter and TRD Pro target customers with different preferences, and giving them choices is the best way of making the Sequoia more relevant in this particular segment. SR5 Trailhunter customers get Old Man Emu suspension, underbody protection, front recovery hooks, Michelin LTX Trail rubber boots, exclusive bronze wheels for said tires, and Trailhunter badging where it matters.
Crawl Control, Multi-Terrain Select, and a locking rear differential are on the menu as well, managing traction over a variety of surfaces. Unfortunately, this package is not compatible with the SR5 Premium package. Why? Beats me, but I do know that prospective customers are missing out on leather-trimmed seats.
At the other end of the spectrum, the TRD Pro takes a different route. For 2027, its maker gave it FOX QS3 adjustable shock absorbers. Red tow hooks and a new Honeycomb signature paint color pretty much complete the model year changes. Of course, ISO-dynamic seats and BBS forged wheels are on the menu as well.
All grades retain the familiar i-FORCE MAX twin-turbo V6 hybrid powertrain, which outputs a combined 437 horsepower and 583 pound-feet (790 Newton-meters) of twist. Being a hybrid, the electric side of the powertrain is especially useful in scenarios where near-instant torque delivery is preferred.
Photo: Toyota The hybrid oomph further enables a maximum towing capacity of 9,520 pounds (4,318 kilograms) when properly equipped for this kind of work. Speaking of towing, 2027 models get a more sophisticated group of trailer assistance tech. Automated Trailer Detection uses radar and the rear camera to detect a connected trailer, estimating its physical characteristics.
Trailer Blind Spot Monitor, Trailer Lane Trace Assist, and Trailer Backup Guide are highlights in their own right. While said features won't make towing completely foolproof, they address the less enjoyable parts of handling a large trailer. Toyota further worked its magic inside, where 14-inch touchscreen infotainment becomes standard across the board.
The instrument cluster is a 12.3-inch unit, and 5G connectivity is handled by AT&T. A built-in Drive Recorder Dash Cam also needs mentioning, for it uses exterior cameras to capture 20-second clips of automatically triggered or manual events. Footage can be reviewed on the center display.
Over-the-air software updates are on the menu as well, as is the Advanced Rear Seat Reminder that detects second- and third-row movement via millimeter-wave radar. When it comes to pricing, Toyota wants $69,900 for the most basic SR5 there is for model year 2027.
Add $2,195 for the destination fee, and you get $72,095 from the outset. Four-wheel drive is now standard, though. The first units should hit dealers this fall.

Magic Cruiser in 2023, Copart Wreck Now: 1969 Pontiac GTO Will Make You Cry, Drivetrain Still Good
47 photos
Photo: Copart
The phrase “1969 Pontiac GTO” immediately evokes images of tire-shredding muscle car dominance, vacuum-operated hidden headlights, a line of angry engineers violently taking turns with the crowbar at the Endura nose, and the psychedelic marketing campaign of The Judge. It represents Detroit’s high-octane golden era at its absolute peak—a period when raw horsepower reigned supreme, and fuel economy wasn't even in the urban vocabulary of gearheads.
As the years march on, finding an unmolested , functional survivor of this legendary breed becomes an event worth celebrating. Finding one that was recently saved, cherished, and then violently totaled to the Happy Driving Planes? Well, that just breaks a gearhead's heart.
Such is the tragic tale of one specific 1969 Pontiac GTO Hardtop Coupe – the very one in the gallery. Back in 2023, this pristine piece of American automotive history was a proud showroom star at Classic Car Addict in Mesa, Arizona. It wasn't a trailer queen, but rather a beautifully maintained, highly honest "driver-quality" example finished in striking Matador Red over a matching red vinyl bucket-seat interior.
It was as loud visually as it was mechanically. Packing a numbers-matching 400-cubic-inch V8, a crisp Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 3-speed automatic transmission, a functional hood-mounted tachometer, and power front disc brakes, it was the ultimate turnkey classic cruiser. At the time, the odometer showed a mere 43,331 original miles. It was listed and sold in the ballpark of $45,000 to $50,000—a fair price for a muscle car icon ready to rule the local drive-in.
Photo: Copart Fast forward to 2026, and the car’s fortunes have taken a devastating turn. After adding less than 1,500 miles under its new owner, bringing the odometer to 44,814 miles, disaster struck. The GTO was involved in a severe rear-end collision. The violent impact caved in the rear valance, crumpled the quarter panels, and twisted the rear subframe of the historic A-body.
Given the skyrocketing costs of vintage sheet metal, specialized frame straightening, and flawless Matador Red paint, insurance adjusters did what they do best: they crunched the numbers, shook their heads, and branded it a total loss. Today, the car sits in an insurance salvage yard, listed on Copart in Andrews, Texas, as a sad, upcoming lot waiting for a brave restorer or a dismantler looking for its intact, standard 350-horsepower drivetrain.
To appreciate what was lost, we ought to dive into the history of the legendary "Goat." The GTO moniker debuted in late 1963 as an optional performance package for the 1964 Pontiac Le Mans, effectively birth-mothering the true American muscle car craze. John DeLorean, Pontiac’s ambitious chief engineer, broke GM’s internal rules by stuffing an optional 389-cubic-inch V8 into an intermediate platform.
Photo: Copart It was glorious, rebellious, and against what GM had just forbidden – namely, intermediates with a displacement-to-weight ratio larger numerically than 1:10 (cubic inches per pound).
The gamble paid off massively. The GTO became a standalone model in 1966, launching its iconic first generation, which lasted through 1967. The heavily redesigned, fastback-styled second generation took over from 1968 to 1972, followed by the single-year Colonnade-styled third generation in 1973.
By 1974, the GTO shrunk to a compact Ventura-based option package before the nameplate was shelved, only to return briefly thirty years later as a captive import from Holden between 2004 and 2006.
Production numbers over the GTO's classic run paint a picture of immense popularity that gradually succumbed to rising insurance premiums and emissions mandates. In its debut year of 1964, Pontiac sold 32,450 packages. That number skyrocketed to 75,352 in 1965, peaked at an incredible 96,946 units in 1966, and held strong at 81,722 for 1967.
Photo: Copart The second-generation restyle brought 87,684 buyers into showrooms for 1968. By 1969—the model year of our doomed protagonist—production sat at 72,287 units. From there, the slide was steep: 40,149 units in 1970; 10,532 in 1971; 5,807 in 1972; the all-time low of 4,806 in 1973; and 7,058 in 1974.
Isolating our tragic Copart survivor within the 1969 model year reveals its exact place in the production hierarchy. Out of the 72,287 GTOs built that year, the vast majority were pillarless Hardtop Coupes like this one, accounting for 58,126 units (compared to just 7,328 convertibles and 6,833 fixed-post sports coupes).
When you narrow it down by powertrain, the standard, base 400-cubic-inch V8 pushing 350 horsepower outpaced the high-revving Ram Air III and Ram Air IV options. Paired with General Motors' ubiquitous 3-speed Turbo 400 automatic transmission, this exact mechanical configuration accounted for roughly 24,000 of the hardtops built. Furthermore, its "R" plant code confirms it was stamped out of the Arlington, Texas assembly facility.
Photo: Copart Back in 1969, rolling out of a Pontiac dealership in a base GTO Hardtop Coupe required a financial commitment of around $3,156 before options. Adding the automatic transmission, power disc brakes, a radio, and the iconic hood tach pushed the original window sticker closer to $3,800. In the 2023 market, a clean, highly original, driver-qualit y GTO like this one commanded anywhere from $45,000 to $50,000.
Now, its fate hangs in the balance on a Copart auction block. While the rear sheet metal is utterly destroyed, the car’s front clip, solid interior, and numbers-matching 400 V8 engine remain highly valuable. According to the add, the engine starts and runs, and the transmission engages. The Goat is on life support, but its days are not many upstream, and they will run dry pretty soon.
Whether someone will attempt a painstaking, five-figure frame-off restoration to undo the sins of 2026, or whether this great Goat will simply become a donor to keep other muscle-era survivors alive, remains to be seen. It's a bruising reminder that out on the blacktop, history can be erased in a fraction of a second.

source_document.body:
The cargo division of Middle East carrier Emirates has introduced a dedicated product designed to facilitate the shipping process for cloud computing companies and suppliers with time-critical AI-related products, which have become a major driver of air cargo demand in the past year.
The product combines priority loading, specialized handling to keep equipment upright and minimize risk of damage, and proactive airport-to-airport shipment monitoring for server racks, semiconductors, graphics processing units and other critical hardware, the airline said in a news release this week.
Why It Matters: The rapid adoption of AI technologies and construction of data centers has lifted revenues for large logistics companies and airlines, which view hyperscalers as a big growth opportunity . AI-related goods such as semiconductors and data-transmission equipment have become a major driver of international trade growth. Shipments of electronics and equipment needed for server farms have contributed mightily to the 5% to 6% growth in air cargo traffic, year-to-date through October, offsetting declines in e-commerce volume.
Large-scale deployments typically involve high-value cargo, compressed timelines and specialized handling requirements, with much of the demand involving intra-Asia shipments between suppliers and manufacturers, and exports from Asia to other parts of the world. Japan Airlines recently began chartering Boeing 747 cargo jets to support freight forwarder Nippon Express, which needed dedicated capacity for technology clients.
In July alone, Emirates SkyCargo said it transported more than 700 metric tons of AI infrastructure across its global network.
Emirates SkyCargo said AI Tech also offers higher levels of operational oversight and communication to ensure deliveries meet demanding customer specifications as it strives to attract more Big Tech business.
Emirates SkyCargo operates a fleet of 19 Boeing 777-200 production freighters and one 777-300 converted freighter. With more 777 passenger aircraft scheduled for conversion to full cargo configuration, it expects to have 23 dedicated cargo jets by March. SkyCargo also manages cargo moved in the belly of Emirates’ large fleet of passenger aircraft, but the freighters are best equipped to handle tall and dense server racks that often weigh more than 3.8 tons.
